Alice employed Bob on 12 occasions in 2017 spanning 11 different calendar weeks (weeks 04, 05, 09, 11, 13, 19, 41, 43, 45, 47, 48), meeting the 10 different-weeks threshold. The only risk is if the "preceding calendar year" provision changes the calculation, but since all employments occurred in 2017, the statute applies directly.

Let me analyze the situation:

Section 3306(a)(1)(B) states that an "employer" is someone who "on each of some 10 days during the calendar year or during the preceding calendar year, each day being in a different calendar week, employed at least one individual in employment for some portion of the day."

The facts show Alice employed Bob on 12 occasions in 2017:
- Jan 24, 2017 (Week 04)
- Feb 4, 2017 (Week 05)
- Mar 3, 2017 (Week 09)
- Mar 18, 2017 (Week 11)
- Apr 1, 2017 (Week 13)
- May 9, 2017 (Week 19)
- Oct 14, 2017 (Week 41)
- Oct 25, 2017 (Week 43)
- Nov 8, 2017 (Week 45)
- Nov 22, 2017 (Week 47)
- Dec 1, 2017 (Week 48)
- Dec 2, 2017 (Week 48)

I count the distinct weeks: 04, 05, 09, 11, 13, 19, 41, 43, 45, 47, 48 = 11 distinct weeks.

So Alice employed Bob on 12 days that fall into 11 different calendar weeks (Dec 1 and Dec 2 are in the same week, week 48).

The requirement is "on each of some 10 days... each day being in a different calendar week." Since there are 11 different weeks represented, this means Alice employed Bob on at least 10 days, each in a different calendar week.

Therefore, Section 3306(a)(1)(B) applies to Alice for 2017, and the answer is Entailment.
